talks.title: Device Code Phishing Is Dead, Long Live New Azure AD Attacks!
talks.teaser: Elias Issa examines Device Code Phishing Is Dead, Long Live New Azure AD Attacks!.
talks.summary:
Overview: Elias, head of red team at Orange Cyberdefense, presents at Insomni'hack on new Azure AD attack vectors beyond device code phishing, including techniques validated in four red team operations.

Key Topics: Azure AD authentication mechanisms and their attack surfaces; device code phishing limitations; new social engineering vectors for token theft; password spraying effectiveness; and coordination with Microsoft on disclosure.

Technical Details: Elias demonstrates attack flows where victims receive codes to enter on legitimate Microsoft sites, completing authentication including MFA. He also covers password spraying against valid email lists with common passwords, noting its continued effectiveness despite visibility.

Takeaways: Azure AD's diverse authentication options create multiple attack paths beyond device code phishing. Organizations should monitor for anomalous authentication patterns and enforce strong password policies.

talks.title: Unmasking A Novel Google Drive Phishing Chain
talks.teaser: Bobby Rauch analyzes Unmasking A Novel Google Drive Phishing Chain.
talks.summary:
Personal Discovery of the Campaign

The speaker, an Amazon offensive security engineer presenting personally, recounts receiving a Google Drive iOS push notification warning his storage was nearly full—a believable premise because his Drive actually was full. The notification originated from a random Micah Dean account on driaz.onmicrosoft.com, not Google.

Attacker Infrastructure Patterns

Threat actors easily spin up Microsoft 365 tenants with multiple onmicrosoft.com domains, rotating burned infrastructure. Guardz tracking shows large numbers of randomly generated tenants used for phishing. The HTML storage alert leads victims through a multi-step chain rather than a simple email link.

Evasion and Payload Delivery

To evade email security, attackers host lures on S3 objects with redirectors pointing to pages such as cloudstoragecentral.com hosted in Moldova, correlating with UNC5537 activity. Victims clicking secure storage are pushed toward Total Drive installers whose pre- and post-install scripts can hide malicious payloads, illustrating how trusted cloud brands cloak affiliate scam delivery.

talks.title: Cybersecurity Between Geopolitics And Tech Supremacy
talks.teaser: Florian Schütz investigates Cybersecurity Between Geopolitics And Tech Supremacy.
talks.summary:
Flawed Attack-Defense Framing

A Swiss federal defense speaker argues pure “we are attacked, we must defend” thinking puts defenders on a losing budget curve. Effective strategy also raises attacker costs—most incidents are criminal enterprises sensitive to ROI—and accepts breaches while shaping cheaper, resilient environments.

From Dot-Com Optimism to Geopolitics

Cyberspace was once framed economically after the dot-com boom, echoing John Perry Barlow’s Davos declaration that technology democratizes and frees cyberspace from government. Snowden-era revelations and great-power competition shifted technology policy toward security, intelligence, and control of networks.

Semiconductor and AI Supremacy

Modern flashpoints include AI productivity, 5G reach, and fab concentration—only TSMC and Samsung make leading chips; ASML dominates lithography tools. Geopolitical imperatives now push regionalized supply chains, US/EU fab investments, AI weapons/surveillance uses, and attempts to deny rivals access to advanced stacks.

Europe’s Strategic Choices

Europe lacks a full independent tech stack versus US and Chinese ecosystems; building one would take decades. The speaker notes European strengths in analog chips for guided weapons, urges realistic AI power constraints, and warns digital sovereignty rhetoric often ignores economic and energy limits.

talks.title: Livestreaming From North Korea's IT Workers Laptop Farm
talks.teaser: Mauro Eldritch analyzes Livestreaming From North Korea's IT Workers Laptop Farm.
talks.summary:
North Korean IT worker threat

Mauro and Einar Garcia Perez at Insomnihack detail Famous Chollima, a Lazarus-linked unit conducting remote IT worker fraud, corporate espionage, and revenue generation for the DPRK regime across finance, healthcare, engineering, and expanding sectors including real estate and pharma.

Honeypot operation

In a first-of-its-kind sting with Finers, BCIT, and ANY.RUN, they built a fake laptop farm/sandbox mimicking contractor environments, monitored GitHub recruitment spam, infiltrated handler networks, and recorded operatives from initial login through job-scam attempts.

GitHub tradecraft

Stage one tracked GitHub spammers using repetitive outreach templates, cloned profile images, rapid follower inflation, and clustering of related accounts. Stage two containment observed full attacker behavior inside isolated ANY.RUN laptop sandboxes, yielding technical indicators for defenders hiring remote developers.

talks.title: SACL: The Detection Capability You've Been Ignoring
talks.teaser: Wojtek Sochacki examines SACL: The Detection Capability You've Been Ignoring.
talks.summary:
## Overview
Marouane Aloui and Wojtek argue SOC teams overlook Windows System Access Control Lists (SACLs)—built-in auditing that closes EDR visibility gaps.

## EDR Blind Spots
Endpoint tools excel at writes and deletes but often miss file reads, subtle Active Directory object access, and policy differences across agent versions—gaps discovered painfully mid-incident.

## SACL Mechanics
Unlike DACLs (who may access an object), SACLs log allowed and denied attempts to the Security event log—like cameras recording every door try. They apply to files, registry keys, and AD objects without extra agents.

## Takeaways
Detection engineering should instrument high-value assets with SACLs for read/access auditing, complementing EDR rather than waiting on vendor roadmaps.

talks.title: Adversary Tracking And All The Lies We Tell Ourselves by Joe Slowik
talks.teaser: Presenters detail vulnerability discovery and exploitation in Adversary Tracking And All The Lies We Tell Ourselves by Joe Slowik.
talks.summary:
## Overview

In the presentation *"Adversary Tracking And All The Lies We Tell Ourselves,"* Joe Slowik—head of threat detection/intelligence development, detection engineering, and threat hunting at Huntress, as well as founder of Perales—examines how the cybersecurity industry defines and conceptualizes threat actors. Slowik argues that traditional mental models and industry tropes surrounding adversaries are often overly simplistic and fail to reflect the operational realities of modern offensive campaigns.

## Defining the "Adversary"

Slowik contrasts common cultural tropes—such as the stereotypical hoodie-wearing hacker, official state-sponsored wanted posters, or flamboyant e-crime figures posing with Lamborghinis—with standard industry definitions. Referencing the National Institute of Standards and Technology (NIST), an adversary is formally defined as:

* A person, group, organization, or government that conducts or has the intent to conduct detrimental activities against an entity.

While many in the security community use the word "attack," Slowik highlights that NIST's phrasing of "detrimental activities" is intentional, noting that "attack" can be unnecessarily narrow or strong for certain cyber activities.

## The Myth of the Monolithic Threat Actor

A primary flaw in contemporary threat intelligence is the assumption that adversaries (such as Lazarus Group, Conti, Equation Group, or APT28) operate as unified, monolithic single entities handling every phase of an operation. 

Slowik explains that modern offensive operations—whether state-sponsored, criminal, or even red team/penetration testing—are fundamentally complex and specialized:

* **Specialization and Division of Labor:** Single individuals or groups rarely manage every stage of the cyber kill chain or fill out every category in the MITRE ATT&CK matrix alone. Doing everything in-house is inefficient and impractical.
* **Cooperation and Ecosystems:** Operators rely on teams with specialized skill sets. Different entities specialize in developing malware, managing infrastructure, or executing initial access, and then interoperate, collaborate, or broker/sell access to other actors.
* **Separation of Roles:** In state-centric and organized cyber environments, operations are structured with distinct layers: an overriding authority or customer providing strategic direction and mission objectives, distinct groups responsible for developing technical capabilities and writing malware, and dedicated operators executing the intrusion.

## Key Takeaways for Security Disciplines

Treating sophisticated adversaries as single, monolithic actors creates blind spots for defenders. Understanding the distributed nature of modern cyber operations—disentangling capability developers, access brokers, and operators—is essential not only for threat intelligence analysts, but also for detection development, red teaming, and adversary emulation exercises.

talks.title: Permissionless Android Universal Overlays by Dimitrios Valsamaras
talks.teaser: Security researchers examine technical aspects of Permissionless Android Universal Overlays by Dimitrios Valsamaras.
talks.summary:
Overview:
Dimitrios Valsamaras, Senior Security Researcher at Microsoft Threat Intelligence and former Google Play Store malware review lead, presents research on universal Android overlay attacks that require no permissions. The presentation analyzes Android's graphics architecture, window management lifecycle, and the historical evolution of UI confusion and tapjacking attacks. Valsamaras demonstrates how systemic design behaviors in window management and backward-compatibility mechanisms allow malicious applications to display deceptive overlays over victim apps without declaring or requesting the sensitive SYSTEM_ALERT_WINDOW permission.

Key Topics:
- Android graphics stack architecture (View, Surface, WindowManagerService, SurfaceFlinger, Hardware Composer)
- Window Z-ordering, window types, and permission requirements (SDK < 23 backward compatibility)
- Window event dispatching flags (FLAG_NOT_TOUCHABLE click-through behavior)
- Permissionless universal overlay creation and free-floating process-bound windows

Technical Details:
In Android, user interface components (Views) are backed by Surface objects managed by SurfaceFlinger, which coordinates with the Hardware Composer HAL for final on-screen display composition. The ordering, positioning, focus, and lifecycle animations of these surfaces are dictated by the WindowManagerService (WMS). Applications interact with WMS indirectly via WindowManager and WindowManager.LayoutParams. Windows reside along a vertical Z-order axis determined by window types. Historically, high-priority overlay windows (such as TYPE_APPLICATION_OVERLAY or deprecated TYPE_SYSTEM_ALERT) sat atop the Z-axis to display floating elements across the OS, requiring the dangerous SYSTEM_ALERT_WINDOW permission.

The speaker reveals how Android maintains backward compatibility for legacy applications. Prior to Android SDK 23 (Android 6.0 Marshmallow), SYSTEM_ALERT_WINDOW was granted automatically at install time. When modern Android versions run applications targeting SDK versions lower than 23, the platform automatically approves the overlay permission by default. Furthermore, window behavioral flags alter how input events are processed. By applying FLAG_NOT_TOUCHABLE, an overlay window instructs the window manager to ignore user touches and transparently dispatch click events to whatever underlying window sits below, enabling stealthy click-through tapjacking without requiring special user-facing permissions.

Windows added through WindowManager.addView() exhibit process-level persistence rather than activity-level coupling. Once created, these free-floating windows remain active on screen even after the originating application's Activity is dismissed, as long as the parent background process remains alive. Threat actors and Android banking malware exploit this decoupling alongside unprivileged window types to create universal overlays without user notification. By synchronizing overlay instantiation with background task-switching telemetry, a permissionless malware app can project deceptive authentication prompts or disguise malicious consent dialogues over legitimate banking, corporate, or system applications.

Key Takeaways:
Android application developers must harden sensitive activities by setting filterTouchesWhenObscured to true to prevent obscured touch dispatching and tapjacking attacks. Operating system vendors must restrict backward compatibility affordances, strictly enforcing runtime permission checks even for apps targeting legacy SDKs below level 23. Mobile threat detection solutions must monitor process-bound floating windows and correlate WindowManager calls with background application states to detect unauthorized UI overlays.

(AI summary — Gemini Flash)

talks.title: Using Artificial Intelligence to Predict Malicious Infrastructure Activity
talks.teaser: Staffan Truvé details Using Artificial Intelligence to Predict Malicious Infrastructure Activity.
talks.summary:
Overview: Much of next-gen AV relies on machine learning to generalize to never-before-seen malware. Less well appreciated, however, is that machine learning can be susceptible to attack by, ironically, other machine learning models. In this talk, we demonstrate an AI agent trained through reinforcement learning to modify malware to evade machine learning malware detection. Reinforcement learning has produced game-changing AI's that top human level performance in the game of Go and a myriad of hacked retr

Key Topics: o Atari games (e.g., Pong). In an analogous fashion, we demonstrate an AI agent that has learned through thousands of "games" against a next-gen AV malware detector which sequence of functionality-preserving changes to perform on a Windows PE malware file so that it bypasses the detector. No math or machine learning background is required; fundamental understanding of malware and Windows PE files is a welcome; and previous experience hacking Atari Pong is a plus.
